title: How much is it?
title_target: เท่าไหร่ครับ — Thâo-rài khráp
goal: Count from zero to a million, ask prices, bargain politely, and understand your change — including the three quirks of Thai numbers that make people mishear prices.
bekal: ask prices with เท่าไหร่
bargain with ลดหน่อยได้ไหม
say expensive, cheap, and "I'll take it at this price"

dialogs.title: บทสนทนา — At Chatuchak market, a T-shirt stall
dialogs.intro: Nok takes Budi shopping on the weekend. Notice that bargaining in Thailand isn't a fight: it happens with a smile, and it stops as soon as one side says ไม่ได้.

notes: **เท่าไหร่ thâo-rài asks about a price or an amount you don't count one by one.** It always goes at the **end** of the sentence: *อันนี้เท่าไหร่* (how much is this), *ทั้งหมดเท่าไหร่* (how much altogether). Compare *กี่ kìi*, which asks **how many items** and is always followed by a classifier: *กี่คน* (how many people), *กี่บาท* (how many baht).

**บาท bàat is Thailand's currency**, and it works as its own classifier. The number attaches directly: *ห้าสิบบาท* (fifty baht). In fast speech *บาท* is often dropped altogether — people just say *ห้าสิบ* and everyone understands.

**ลด lót means "to reduce", and it's the key word for bargaining.** The full sentence is *ลดหน่อยได้ไหม* — "could you go a bit lower?". The word *หน่อย nàwy* in the middle is a softener; without it the sentence sounds like an order.

**ต่อ tàw means "to bargain".** *ต่อได้ไหม tàw dâai mǎi* = "can I bargain?". ⚠️ The unwritten rule: **at markets and street stalls, bargaining is normal; at malls, convenience stores, and restaurants, never.** Bargaining in the wrong place confuses the seller rather than offending them.
**ละ lá means "per".** *ตัวละสองร้อย* = two hundred each, *คนละร้อย* = a hundred per person, *วันละสองครั้ง* = twice a day. The order is: **classifier + ละ + price**.
**ทอน thawn is change (money).** The seller will say *ทอนหกสิบบาทค่ะ*. If you need to ask for your change: *ขอเงินทอนด้วยครับ khǎaw ngoen-thawn dûai khráp*.
**เอา ao means "to take", and it's the most common way to say "I'll have this".** It sounds perfectly normal, not rude — but for something softer use *ขอ khǎaw* (may I have), covered in Unit 6.
**งั้น ngán = "in that case"**, short for *ถ้างั้น thâa-ngán*. It comes up a lot in bargaining, when one side adjusts the offer.

grammars.title: Numbers: the whole system in one table
body: Thai counts much like English — ones, tens, hundreds, built up from left to right — with three exceptions marked below the table.

head: Number
Thai
Pronunciation
Number
Thai
Pronunciation
rows: ยี่สิบเอ็ด
หนึ่งหมื่น

after: ⚠️ **Quirk 1 — เอ็ด èt replaces หนึ่ง in the ones place from 11 up.** 11 = *สิบเอ็ด*, 21 = *ยี่สิบเอ็ด*, 101 = *ร้อยเอ็ด*. *หนึ่ง* is still used for the number one on its own.
⚠️ **Quirk 2 — 20 is ยี่สิบ *yîi-sìp*, not สองสิบ.** Only twenty works this way; 30, 40, 50 are all regular.

⚠️ **Quirk 3 — หมื่น *mùuen* (10,000) and แสน *sǎaen* (100,000) have no English equivalent.** 50,000 baht is *ห้าหมื่นบาท* (five × ten-thousand), not counted in thousands. This is the number-one reason foreigners mishear rents and salaries.

after: ⚠️ *ถูก thùuk* has two completely different meanings: **cheap** and **correct**. *ถูกต้อง thùuk-tâwng* always means "correct"; *ถูก* on its own in a shopping context almost always means "cheap".
QR payment (*พร้อมเพย์ phráawm-phee*) is now used everywhere, even by street vendors. *สแกนได้ไหมครับ* is often more useful than asking about cards.

blocks.text: Thai prices are read straight from left to right, just as in English. The only thing to practice is speed.

blocks.text: Note that *หนึ่ง* in front of *ร้อย, พัน, หมื่น* is usually **dropped** in conversation: 120 is more often *ร้อยยี่สิบ* than *หนึ่งร้อยยี่สิบ*.

blocks.title: If you didn't catch the price
items: **พูดอีกทีได้ไหมครับ/คะ** *phûut ìik thii dâai mǎi* — could you say that again?

**เขียนให้หน่อยได้ไหมครับ/คะ** *khǐan hâi nàwy dâai mǎi* — could you write it down? This is the most powerful trick at a market; almost every vendor has a calculator and will type the number right in.
**พูดช้าๆ ได้ไหมครับ/คะ** *phûut cháa-cháa dâai mǎi* — could you speak slowly?

blocks.text: Bargaining in Thailand has an unwritten limit of politeness, and crossing it doesn't make people angry — it just makes them go quiet and refuse with a smile, which is actually worse.

items: **Aim about 10-20 percent lower, not half.** Offering half price is a habit from other countries and here sounds like an insult to the goods.
**Smile.** Bargaining with a serious face turns it into a fight, and Thais avoid fights by simply not selling to you.
**Buying more than one is your best bargaining tool.** *เอาสองตัว ลดได้ไหมคะ* almost always works.
**If the seller says ไม่ได้ *mâi dâai* — stop.** That isn't the start of a new round; it's the final answer, delivered as politely as possible.
**Don't bargain if you don't intend to buy.** This is the mistake that sours the mood most.

blocks.title: Four bargaining lines, from gentle to firm
items: **ลดหน่อยได้ไหมครับ/คะ** — could you go a bit lower? (safest)
**สองร้อยได้ไหมครับ/คะ** — would two hundred be okay? (naming your own price)
**ถ้าเอาสองอัน ลดได้ไหมครับ/คะ** — if I take two, can you go lower?
**แพงไปหน่อยครับ/ค่ะ** — it's a bit too expensive. Said with a smile, this often gets the seller to drop the price without being asked.
